title: Argue Both Sides
description: In each round, you're assigned a position — FOR or AGAINST — on a controversial motion. You must argue it convincingly, even if you disagree. True adaptability means arguing any side with integrity.
coaching_moment: The most intellectually agile people can argue any position well — not because they have no values, but because they understand multiple perspectives deeply. Arguing both sides builds empathy, sharpens logic, and reveals the complexity in every issue.

rounds.title: Motion: AI Should Replace Teachers
rounds.scenario: You've been assigned to argue FOR: AI should replace human teachers. You have 90 seconds. Which argument is strongest?

choices.label: AI provides personalized learning at scale impossible for any single teacher
choices.outcome: Strong utilitarian argument. Addresses the scalability gap in global education.

choices.label: AI removes bias in grading and feedback
choices.outcome: Valid but narrow. Doesn't address the relationship dimension of teaching.

choices.label: Students actually prefer AI tutors because they're non-judgmental
choices.outcome: Interesting psychological angle. Supported by some research.

rounds.coaching_moment: Arguing FOR a position you may not hold requires intellectual honesty: find the best version of the argument, not a strawman. This is called steel-manning.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Motion: AI Should Replace Teachers — AGAINST
rounds.scenario: Now argue AGAINST: AI should replace teachers. Same motion, opposite side. What's your strongest counter?

choices.label: Teaching is fundamentally relational — AI cannot provide emotional mentorship
choices.outcome: Core of the counter-argument. Human connection is irreplaceable in development.

choices.label: AI systems replicate existing biases rather than eliminating them
choices.outcome: Technical counter. Strong but requires evidence to be compelling.

choices.label: Teachers model how to be human — that can't be automated
choices.outcome: Philosophical argument. Powerful for audiences who value humanistic education.

rounds.coaching_moment: You just argued both sides. Notice how you felt. The discomfort of defending a position you disagree with is where intellectual growth happens.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Motion: Social Media Does More Harm Than Good — FOR
rounds.scenario: Argue FOR: Social media does more harm than good. Best opening argument?

choices.label: Algorithmic amplification of outrage systematically degrades democratic discourse
choices.outcome: Sophisticated structural argument. Goes beyond individual harm to systemic effects.

choices.label: Teenage depression has increased in direct correlation with smartphone adoption
choices.outcome: Data-driven argument. Strong but correlation-causation caveat required.

choices.label: Social media creates echo chambers that increase polarization
choices.outcome: Well-evidenced. But your opponent may have counter-evidence.

rounds.coaching_moment: The strongest FOR argument focuses on systemic effects, not anecdotes. Systems thinking elevates the quality of any argument.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Motion: Social Media Does More Harm Than Good — AGAINST
rounds.scenario: Now argue AGAINST. What's the most compelling counter to the harm narrative?

choices.label: Social media enabled social movements that wouldn't have organized otherwise (#MeToo, Arab Spring)
choices.outcome: Historical evidence of positive structural impact. Hard to dismiss.

choices.label: The problem is misuse, not the technology itself — we regulate cars, not ban them
choices.outcome: Policy analogy. Reframes the motion from banning to regulating.

choices.label: For marginalized communities, social media is their primary access to information and community
choices.outcome: Empathy-forward argument. Centers voices often left out of harm-centric debates.

rounds.coaching_moment: The strongest AGAINST argument doesn't deny harm — it reframes what the real question is. That's intellectual judo.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Motion: Standardized Testing Should Be Abolished — FOR
rounds.scenario: Argue FOR abolishing standardized tests. Best case?

choices.label: Tests measure test-taking skill, not intelligence or potential — they advantage the wealthy
choices.outcome: Equity argument. Directly challenges the validity of what's being measured.

choices.label: High-stakes tests create teaching to the test, narrowing curriculum
choices.outcome: Pedagogical argument. Well-supported by teacher surveys and outcomes data.

choices.label: Finland abolished standardized tests and has world-leading education outcomes
choices.outcome: International comparison argument. Strong but Finland's context differs significantly.

rounds.coaching_moment: Equity arguments are powerful because they challenge whether the system is fair at its foundation, not just at its edges.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Motion: Standardized Testing Should Be Abolished — AGAINST
rounds.scenario: Now argue AGAINST abolishing standardized testing. Best defense of tests?

choices.label: Without objective measures, admissions favor soft skills which privilege those with social capital
choices.outcome: Counter-intuitive equity argument. Tests may be the only pathway for underrepresented merit.

choices.label: Standardized tests provide accountability and common benchmarks across diverse schools
choices.outcome: Systems argument. Without common measures, quality assurance becomes impossible.

choices.label: The problem is score misuse, not the tests themselves — reform, don't abolish
choices.outcome: Moderate position. Often the most defensible in practice.

rounds.coaching_moment: The AGAINST position on equity grounds reveals that complex issues have equity arguments on BOTH sides. Intellectual humility means holding that complexity.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Final: Your Real View
rounds.scenario: Final round. No assigned side. Across all motions: what is YOUR actual view on one of them — and how has arguing both sides changed your thinking?

choices.label: My view has shifted — I understand the opposing side better now
choices.outcome: Intellectual growth demonstrated. This is the goal of the exercise.

choices.label: My view is the same but I can now explain why the other side is wrong
choices.outcome: Understanding without agreement is valid. You've strengthened your own position by stress-testing it.

choices.label: I'm now less certain than before — both sides have genuine merit
choices.outcome: The most intellectually honest response. Complexity is not weakness; it's wisdom.

rounds.coaching_moment: The ability to hold genuine uncertainty — not as indecision, but as intellectual respect for complexity — is the mark of a sophisticated thinker. You've earned it.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Reflection: The Steel-Manning Principle
rounds.scenario: Steel-manning means arguing the BEST version of an opposing view, not the weakest. Which of these is a steel-man of a view you personally disagree with?

choices.label: Those who want tighter immigration controls worry about wage competition for the most vulnerable workers — a genuine equity concern
choices.outcome: Steel-man acknowledged. You can disagree with the conclusion while respecting the underlying concern.

choices.label: People who doubt climate change are just stupid or in denial
choices.outcome: Strawman, not steel-man. This explains nothing and changes no one's mind.

choices.label: Conservatives who resist welfare expansion fear dependency culture — a legitimate concern about incentive structures
choices.outcome: Steel-man. Understands the logic behind a position you may oppose.

rounds.coaching_moment: Steel-manning is not agreement — it's the prerequisite for genuine disagreement. You can only truly oppose a view you first genuinely understand.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

reflection_prompt: Which motion was hardest to argue on your assigned side? What made it difficult — and what did that difficulty reveal?
learning_objectives: Develop critical thinking through rounds gameplay
Build self-awareness about your strengths and areas for growth

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Argue Both Sides Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 4 rounds of Argue Both Sides. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.
